newsitem.title: USA: CBOT soybeans end mixed, weather boosts old crop.
newsitem.headline: CBOT soybeans end mixed, weather boosts old crop.

text.p: CBOT soybean futures ended mixed on Friday with nearbys higher on a late short covering rally tied to conflicting weather forecasts, traders said.

"While the local forecasts for all these little areas only have (rainfall) of about 1/2 inch with 30 to 40 percent coverage, if you look at the private forecasters, some were saying 70 percent coverage of 1/2 inch to an inch," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities in Iowa.
Trade sources said revised forecasts issued after noon suggested the heaviest rains would fall to the north of a few dry pockets in central Illinois and eastern Iowa.
Weather Services Corp said there was no sign of any prolonged period of hot, dry weather developing but added that more rain would benefit the crop in parts of central Illinois and eastern Iowa.
Roose and others said shorts were uncomfortable holding a position going into the weekend with uncertain forecasts.
Persistent hot, dry weather could damage corn and soybean crops. July is viewed as a critical month for corn development while August is the key period for soybeans, traders said.
Soybeans ended 6-1/2 cents per bushel higher to 5-1/4 lower with August up four at $7.50.
"There's probably more risk to the upside than down," Roose said, referring to the short covering rally.

Soybeans had struggled much of the session with indications demand for old crop supplies was waning. The National Oilseed Processors Association on Friday put the weekly crush at 23 million bushels, below expectations for 23.5 to 24.5 million bushels.
Cash merchants said basis levels in the country weakened, as did U.S. Gulf CIF values, suggesting to many that demand was tapering off.

The U.S. Agriculture Department's supply and demand data influenced opening trade but was then largely ignored, traders said. USDA cut its old crop ending stocks forecast to 125 million bushels from 130 million. But new crop ending stocks were estimated at 285 million bushels, up from 240 million last month, USDA said.
Traders said the increase was expected after USDA last week forecast soybean acreage at a hefty 70.85 million acres.

But Roose noted USDA left yield unchanged at 38.5 bushels per acre. "They took the cautious approach with the yield at 38.5 bushels," he said. "What that tells the trade is walk a little slower until we can see what the weather is going to do."

On the day, volume was said to be thin. Commercials were on both sides of the market with ADM, Cargill Inc, Produce Grain and Term Commodities small buyers of the August while Produce, Term and Continental Grain were also sellers.

In options trade, FIMAT Futures sold 800 January $7.00 calls at 8-1/4 cents, Lind-Waldock bought 500 November $6.00 puts and sold 500 November $5.75 puts at 13-1/2 and Smith Barney bought 200 September $8.00 calls at three cents.
Volatility in the August closed at 41-1/2 percent, up from 39-3/4 on Thursday. The November closed at 22-1/2 percent, up from 20 percent on Thursday.

Soybean futures volume was estimated by CBOT at 55,000 contracts, compared with Thursday's actual volume of 49,357 contracts. Soybean options volume was pegged at 26,000 contracts, against Thursday's 30,846 contracts.
